PARIS, France (CNN) — In a city renowned as the birthplace of the avant-garde, keeping pace with the latest trends can be a challenge. Here is a rough guide to what is hot right now in the French capital.

**Tecktonik**  
Parisian youths have always embraced trends, and the latest dance craze sweeping the city is Tecktonik — a fusion dance style typically paired with spiked hair and neon accessories. Look out for groups of kids dancing outside the Trocadéro. If you are lucky, you might even catch a Tecktonik-versus-breakdance dance-off.

**Le Scrapbooking**  
Scrapbooking is the current craze among Paris’s more sedate residents. Head to Le Temple du Scrap, at 13 Rue Ernest Cresson, for pretty paper supplies, trimmings, ribbons, and all manner of decorative frippery.

**Bike Around Town**  
Much of Paris is walkable, but the city’s inexpensive bike-hire scheme, Vélib’, launched in 2007, makes zipping around even easier. Thousands of bikes are stationed across the city, with docking points located roughly 300 meters apart. The first 30 minutes of any trip are free; you will need a credit card to register for the scheme. Once you have your bike, you are ready to career around the cobbled streets of Montmartre and rattle along the Seine.

**Café Hotspots**  
The classic Parisian image of smoky cafés has now been banished to the pavements, thanks to a smoking ban in bars and restaurants introduced at the end of 2007. Quel dommage! In winter, the most sought-after café spots are those with heated terraces. You can still light up while sipping a petit café crème, but only if you sit outside — so bring a turtleneck and a beret to stay both warm and stylish.

**Massages at the Mosque**  
Paris is home to a large Muslim population, and La Grande Mosquée de Paris, on Rue Geoffroy St. Hilaire, reflects that heritage. From the outside, the building is absolutely stunning; inside, it is even more spectacular. Treat yourself to a massage at the hammam, or Turkish bath, and you could easily imagine you are in Morocco. Afterward, relax in the courtyard with a glass of mint tea. Be sure to check in advance which days are reserved for men and which for women.

**Subway Style**  
Taking the subway in Paris can be a drag. Striking drivers and filthy platforms can make the Métro a misery. But the light at the end of this often dark and dingy tunnel is the Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre stop — more specifically, the Palais Royal entrance. Like many things in Paris, it is a work of art in its own right, created by French artist Jean-Michel Othoniel. His design of brightly colored glass beads is a delight, and nearby Place Colette is an excellent spot for people-watching: pull up a pew and enjoy.

Paris is often celebrated for its timeless elegance, historic cafés, grand boulevards, and world-famous museums, but the city is also constantly changing. Beneath its classic image, new trends and habits continue to shape everyday life, from youth culture and creative hobbies to transport, café customs, and multicultural experiences.

One of the more energetic trends to emerge among Parisian youths is Tecktonik, a dance craze known for its distinctive fusion of styles. Combining fast arm movements, electronic music influences, and elements borrowed from hip-hop and club dancing, Tecktonik quickly became more than just a dance: it developed into a recognizable fashion statement. Its followers often complete the look with spiked hair, bold clothing, and neon accessories, creating a vivid and highly stylized youth subculture on the streets and dance floors of Paris.

For those who prefer a quieter and more creative pastime, scrapbooking has become increasingly popular. Many Parisians have embraced the hobby as a way to preserve memories, decorate personal albums, and create handmade gifts. Specialist shops such as Le Temple Du Scrap provide a wide range of materials, including patterned papers, stickers, stamps, ribbons, and other decorative supplies. These stores cater to both beginners and experienced scrapbookers, offering inspiration for anyone interested in turning photographs and mementos into carefully designed keepsakes.

Exploring Paris has also become easier thanks to the city’s Vélib’ bike-hire scheme. With docking stations located throughout the capital, Vélib’ allows residents and visitors to rent bicycles cheaply and conveniently. It offers a practical alternative to the metro or taxis, especially for short journeys between neighborhoods. Cycling through Paris provides a different perspective on the city, making it possible to move at street level, discover smaller side roads, and enjoy landmarks, parks, and riverbanks at a more relaxed pace.

Café culture, one of Paris’s most famous traditions, has also adapted to changing laws and lifestyles. Since the smoking ban introduced in 2007, smoking has no longer been permitted inside cafés, bars, and restaurants. As a result, many establishments have expanded or improved their outdoor seating areas. Heated terraces have become a familiar sight, allowing smokers to continue enjoying a coffee, a glass of wine, or a conversation outside even during colder months. This change has subtly transformed the atmosphere of Parisian cafés, bringing more life onto the pavements and terraces.

Another distinctive experience in the city can be found at La Grande Mosquée de Paris. With its beautiful architecture, peaceful courtyard, and North African influences, the mosque offers visitors a striking cultural contrast within the French capital. Beyond its religious and architectural significance, it is also known for its hammam, where guests can enjoy traditional steam baths and massages. For those seeking a moment of relaxation, as well as a glimpse into another side of Paris’s cultural diversity, La Grande Mosquée provides a memorable and atmospheric escape.

Together, these examples show that Paris is far more than a city preserved in history. It is a place where youth trends, artistic hobbies, green transport, evolving social customs, and multicultural traditions all exist side by side, adding new layers to the character of the French capital.

# Paris now: retro dance floors, terrace culture and the small pleasures of a city in motion

Paris has always been good at turning everyday life into theater. A coffee becomes a ritual, a commute becomes a bike ride past stone façades, and even a métro entrance can look like a string of oversized glass beads dropped from a surrealist necklace.

For travelers looking beyond the postcard circuit, the city’s coolest experiences are often found in the spaces between monuments: on café terraces, in neighborhood craft shops, inside a steamy hammam, or at nightclubs where a once-viral dance style refuses to disappear completely.

## Ride the city like a Parisian: Vélib’ bikes

One of the easiest ways to feel plugged into Paris is to skip the taxi queue and grab a Vélib’, the city’s public bike-share system. The sturdy green-and-blue bikes — many now electric — are parked at docking stations across the capital and surrounding suburbs.

A good first ride: start near the Canal Saint-Martin, cruise toward République, then drift down toward the Seine. More confident cyclists can follow riverside lanes past the Louvre, the Tuileries and the Eiffel Tower, using the growing network of protected bike paths that has helped make Paris feel less car-dominated than it once was.

Tip: Download the Vélib’ app before you go, check that the bike is properly released, and if you’re new to Paris traffic, stick to dedicated lanes and river routes.

## The terrace is the new living room

France’s indoor smoking ban changed the way Parisian cafés look and feel. Since smoking moved outside, terraces have become even more central to the city’s social life — not just in summer, but year-round, with heat lamps, awnings and rows of tiny tables pointed toward the street.

The best terraces are less about famous names than good corners. Look for cafés in the Marais, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Oberkampf, South Pigalle or around Canal Saint-Martin, order a noisette or a glass of wine, and let the city perform.

It is not unusual to see a laptop worker, a first date, a fashion editor, a dog under a chair and three smokers sharing one ashtray — all within a few feet.

## Tecktonik: Paris’s neon dance memory lives on

In the late 2000s, Paris helped launch Tecktonik, the electro dance style known for sharp arm movements, sculpted hair, skinny jeans and futuristic club energy. Its explosive moment as a youth craze has passed, but the aesthetic still flickers through Paris nightlife, retro parties, TikTok nostalgia and electro events.

To catch the spirit, look for electro nights, queer club parties, dance battles or throwback events in neighborhoods like Bastille, Pigalle and the 11th arrondissement. Even if no one is officially calling it “Tecktonik,” you may see traces of its fast, angular style on the dance floor.

Paris has a habit of recycling its own cool. What looks like a throwback one year becomes a trend again the next.

## Scrapbooking and paper shops: Paris for makers

Paris is a dream city for people who travel with a notebook. Beyond luxury boutiques, there is a quieter shopping trail devoted to paper, stamps, stickers, calligraphy, collage and scrapbooking.

Seek out craft and stationery shops around the Marais, the Latin Quarter and near major department stores, where you can find washi tape, handmade papers, rubber stamps, fountain pens, vintage-style labels and decorative notebooks. French paper goods tend to have a particular charm: muted colors, elegant typography and a taste for old-school correspondence.

For a memorable DIY souvenir, collect métro tickets, café receipts, museum stubs, pressed flowers from a market bouquet and photo-booth strips, then build a Paris travel scrapbook as you go. It is a more personal keepsake than another Eiffel Tower keychain.

## Steam, mint tea and calm at the Grande Mosquée hammam

For a break from the city’s hard pavements and museum queues, head to the Grande Mosquée de Paris in the 5th arrondissement. Its hammam is one of the capital’s classic wellness experiences: tiled rooms, warm steam, exfoliation treatments and the sense that time has slowed down.

Afterward, the mosque’s courtyard café is part of the ritual. Order sweet mint tea and North African pastries under the arches, surrounded by mosaic details and greenery. It is one of Paris’s most transporting corners, especially on a gray day.

Before going, check current opening times, reservation rules and gender-specific hours, as hammam access can vary.

## The métro entrance that looks like jewelry

At Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre station, one of Paris’s most photographed métro entrances is not Art Nouveau but contemporary fantasy. “Le Kiosque des Noctambules,” created by artist Jean-Michel Othoniel, rises above the station in colorful Murano glass beads and aluminum.

Installed for the centenary of the Paris Métro, the entrance sits near the Comédie-Française and the Louvre, making it an easy detour between major sights. It is playful, strange and very Parisian in its confidence: a public transit entrance dressed like a work of art.

Pair it with a walk through the Palais Royal gardens, where striped columns, arcades, boutiques and quiet benches offer a calmer alternative to the crowds outside the Louvre.

## How to turn it into a day

Start with coffee on a terrace in the Marais, then browse paper and craft shops for scrapbook supplies. Pick up a Vélib’ and ride toward the Seine, stopping at Palais Royal to see Othoniel’s métro entrance and the gardens.

In the afternoon, head to the Grande Mosquée for the hammam and mint tea. After dinner, look for an electro night or dance event — maybe not a full Tecktonik revival, but Paris after dark still knows how to move its arms, strike a pose and make a trend feel alive again.

Paris’s coolest side is not always new. Sometimes it is a bike, a steam room, a café table, a glittering métro entrance — and a city that keeps remixing itself.

I can’t write exactly in CNN’s house style, but here’s a breezy, late-2000s travel-news-style Paris guide with a polished, tourist-friendly feel.

# What’s Hot in Paris Right Now

Paris may still belong to the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre and the perfectly tied scarf — but look closer and the city is moving to a fresher beat. From TikTok-ready dance floors to bike-lane boulevards and design-forward métro stops, here’s where the French capital feels especially alive.

## Youth dance crazes: from street steps to club floors

Forget the postcard Paris of accordion music and slow waltzes. Young Parisians are dancing to Afrobeat, amapiano, shatta, hip-hop, voguing and whatever sound is currently burning through social feeds.

For a glimpse of the city’s youth culture, look toward **La Place** at Les Halles, a hub for hip-hop arts, or **Le Centquatre** in the 19th arrondissement, where dancers often rehearse in the vast public spaces. Late-night energy spills into clubs and bars around **Bastille**, **Pigalle**, **Belleville** and the **Canal Saint-Martin**, where Paris feels far less buttoned-up than its reputation suggests.

## Shopping: vintage, concept stores and quiet luxury

The shopping map has expanded well beyond the Champs-Élysées. The **Marais** remains a tourist-friendly sweet spot, mixing French labels, independent boutiques, vintage finds and fashionable cafés within easy walking distance.

For trendier browsing, head to **Canal Saint-Martin** and the **10th arrondissement**, where small shops sell minimalist clothing, ceramics, books and design objects. **Merci**, the well-known concept store on Boulevard Beaumarchais, still draws visitors looking for a curated Parisian lifestyle under one roof.

Luxury seekers can make for **La Samaritaine**, beautifully restored near the Seine, or the grand department stores **Galeries Lafayette** and **Printemps** near Opéra. Vintage hunters should check the Marais, Montmartre side streets and kilo shops scattered through the city.

## Cycling: Paris on two wheels

Paris has become a city best seen at handlebar height. The once car-dominated boulevards now include expanding bike lanes, and the city’s **Vélib’** bike-share system makes short rides simple for visitors.

A scenic starter route: ride along the **Seine**, past the Louvre and Île de la Cité, then continue toward the Eiffel Tower. For a more local feel, pedal along the **Canal Saint-Martin** or through the broad paths of the **Bois de Vincennes**.

Just remember: Parisian cyclists move with purpose. Stay alert, use marked lanes when possible and don’t stop suddenly for a photo unless you want a symphony of bicycle bells behind you.

## Cafés: not just espresso anymore

The classic Paris café — cane chairs, tiny tables, people-watching for hours — is still very much alive. But today’s café scene also includes specialty coffee, natural wine bars, hybrid bakeries and laptop-friendly corners.

For old-school atmosphere, try the grand cafés of **Saint-Germain-des-Prés** or a neighborhood terrace in the **11th**. For newer coffee culture, explore spots around **République**, **Le Marais**, **Canal Saint-Martin** and **South Pigalle**.

The modern Paris café order? Maybe a flat white in the morning, a matcha in the afternoon and a glass of pét-nat by evening — preferably while pretending not to watch everyone’s outfit.

## Massages and wellness: the new Paris pause

After pounding cobblestones all day, visitors are increasingly trading another museum line for an hour of calm. Paris now offers everything from elegant hotel spas to Thai massage studios, hammams and Japanese-inspired treatment rooms.

For a classic steam-and-scrub experience, book a hammam session. For something sleeker, look to spa addresses in luxury hotels around **Opéra**, **Saint-Honoré** and the **Left Bank**. Travelers on a tighter budget can find well-reviewed massage studios in the Marais, Bastille and Montparnasse areas.

The Parisian wellness rule is simple: book ahead, arrive on time and let yourself slow down. The city will still be there when you emerge.

## Stylish subway stops: underground Paris with flair

The Paris Métro isn’t just transport — occasionally, it’s theater.

Don’t miss **Arts et Métiers**, where the platform is wrapped in copper like a Jules Verne submarine. **Louvre–Rivoli** offers museum-like displays that hint at the treasures above. **Concorde** turns its tiled walls into a giant word puzzle, while **Cité**, on Île de la Cité, feels moody and cinematic with its globe lamps and deep platforms.

For pure romance, **Abbesses** in Montmartre has one of the city’s most photographed Art Nouveau entrances. Just be warned: it’s deep underground, and the stairs are not for the faint of calf.

## The takeaway

Paris is still elegant, but it’s no museum piece. It dances, cycles, shops vintage, drinks better coffee and turns even a métro ride into a design moment. The trick is to mix the icons with the neighborhoods — and leave enough time between plans to follow the crowd, the music or the smell of fresh bread.

When it is time to pause, do as Parisians do: sit outside. Even in chilly weather, the city’s **heated café terraces** turn people-watching into a year-round activity. Order an espresso, a glass of wine or a chocolat chaud, and linger under the warm lamps while the city flows past. The best terrace is not always the most famous one; sometimes it is the corner café near a market street, where office workers, students and longtime residents share the same small tables.

For a restorative break, visit **La Grande Mosquée de Paris** in the 5th arrondissement. Its courtyard, mosaics and peaceful atmosphere offer a change of rhythm from the bustle outside. The mosque’s tea room is especially popular for mint tea and North African pastries, while the hammam has long been known as a relaxing escape from the urban pace.

Finally, mix old Paris with modern wandering around **Palais Royal - Musée du Louvre**. The metro stop places visitors near the Louvre, the Palais Royal gardens and some of the city’s most elegant arcades. The area is ideal for a stylish stroll: contemporary art installations, historic architecture, boutiques, cafés and hidden corners all sit within a few minutes of one another.

The trendiest Paris is not found in a single district or attraction. It is in the movement between them: a borrowed bike, a terrace in winter, a dance floor after midnight, a cup of mint tea, a quiet shop full of paper and color. In a city famous for preserving its past, the fashionable thing is often simply discovering how Paris lives right now.

counterfactuals.output:
## Paris Now: Street Moves, Scrapbook Finds and a New Café Rhythm

Paris may be timeless, but it is never still. Beyond the postcards of the Eiffel Tower and the Louvre, the city is buzzing with small, stylish shifts: dancers turning monuments into stages, cafés adjusting to a smoke-free era, cyclists claiming more of the boulevards, and Metro stations doubling as underground galleries. For visitors looking to catch the capital in motion, here are some of the trends and hotspots giving Paris its current pulse.

### Trocadéro: Where the Eiffel Tower Gets a Soundtrack

For one of the city’s most energetic free shows, head to the Trocadéro, the wide plaza across the Seine from the Eiffel Tower. By day it is a classic photo stop; by late afternoon and evening, it often becomes a stage for street dancers, roller performers, buskers and freestyle crews.

Hip-hop dancers spin, pop and lock against one of the world’s most famous backdrops, drawing an international crowd with phones in the air and smiles all around. The atmosphere is part performance, part social gathering: tourists pause mid-itinerary, local teens cheer on friends, and the Eiffel Tower sparkles on cue after dark.

Travel tip: Bring a little cash for performers, watch your belongings in the crowd, and linger after sunset for the best mix of music, movement and skyline drama.

### Scrapbooking in the City of Beautiful Paper

Paris has always understood the art of keeping memories, and the city is a dream for scrapbookers, journal keepers and lovers of decorative paper. Beyond museum gift shops and souvenir stands, look for specialist stationery boutiques and craft stores selling patterned papers, stickers, washi tape, rubber stamps, calligraphy pens and vintage-style labels.

The Marais, Saint-Germain-des-Prés and areas around the Grands Boulevards are especially rewarding for a stationery hunt, with shops where wrapping paper looks frame-worthy and notebooks feel almost too elegant to write in. Flea markets and bouquinistes along the Seine can also yield old postcards, maps, prints and book pages perfect for travel journals.

What to buy: Eiffel Tower stamps, Art Nouveau motifs, Paris Metro-themed paper, vintage ticket designs, fountain pens, and chic glue-free photo corners for a polished travel album.

### Bike Hire: Paris on Two Wheels

Paris has become far more bike-friendly in recent years, and hiring a bike is now one of the most enjoyable ways to explore the city. Public bike-share schemes, app-based e-bikes and private rental shops make it easy to ride from riverside paths to neighborhood markets without disappearing underground on the Metro.

The Seine quays are a favorite route, especially between the Eiffel Tower, Musée d’Orsay, Notre-Dame and the Bastille area. Canal Saint-Martin offers a more local, relaxed ride, with cafés, bridges and waterside picnics along the way. For a grander outing, confident cyclists can head toward the Bois de Boulogne or Bois de Vincennes.

Good to know: Bike lanes are expanding, but traffic can still be assertive. Use dedicated lanes where possible, follow signals carefully, and consider an e-bike if you want to cover more ground without arriving at dinner overheated.

### Café Culture After the Smoking Ban

The French café has not lost its soul—it has simply moved some of its smoke outdoors. Since smoking bans changed the rhythm of indoor dining and drinking, Parisian café culture has adapted with typical flair. Interiors are clearer and more comfortable for long lunches, while terraces have become even more central to the city’s social life.

On many boulevards, the terrace is now the true theater: friends meet over espressos, remote workers type beside tiny cups, and travelers practice the noble art of people-watching. In colder months, heaters and blankets keep outdoor tables busy, while in summer the best terrace seats can feel like front-row tickets to Paris itself.

The result is a more international-friendly café experience: non-smokers can breathe more easily inside, smokers gather outdoors, and the ritual of sitting, sipping and watching the world go by remains gloriously intact.

### Hammam Massages: A Warm Escape from the Pavement

After a day of cobblestones, museums and Metro stairs, Paris’s hammams offer a restorative counterpoint to urban intensity. Inspired by North African bathing traditions, hammams combine steam, exfoliation and massage in a setting that feels both social and soothing.

Some of the best-known hammam experiences are connected to historic cultural institutions or tucked into spa addresses around the city. Expect warm tiled rooms, clouds of steam, black soap treatments, vigorous scrubs and massages using fragrant oils. It is less about hushed luxury and more about renewal: you emerge softer, slower and ready for another evening out.

Visitor note: Check booking rules in advance, as some hammams have women-only or men-only times, and customs vary. Bring swimwear if required, and do not schedule anything too ambitious immediately afterward—you may want to drift.

### Metro Station Art: The Underground Museum

Paris’s Metro is not just transport; it is also an accidental art tour. Many stations have distinctive designs that reflect the neighborhood above or the history of the city itself. Skip the taxi occasionally and ride with your eyes open.

Arts et Métiers is a favorite, with its copper-toned, submarine-like interior inspired by machinery and invention. Louvre-Rivoli displays replicas and museum-style cases that nod to the treasures nearby. Concorde turns language into design, its tiled walls covered with letters spelling out the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Abbesses, one of the deepest stations in the network, offers a classic Art Nouveau entrance at street level, while newer stations and renovated platforms bring photography, murals and contemporary design into the commute.

For international visitors, the Metro is more than a way to save time. It is a moving map of Parisian identity: revolutionary, artistic, literary, industrial and always a little theatrical.

### The Takeaway: Paris Is Best Between the Icons

Yes, see the Eiffel Tower. Yes, visit the museums. But the most memorable Paris moments often happen in between: a dance battle at Trocadéro, a perfect sheet of marbled paper, a bike ride beside the Seine, a terrace table in the new smoke-light café era, a hammam steam session, or a Metro platform that feels like a secret exhibition.

Paris is still Paris—but look closely, and you will find a city constantly remixing itself.

# What’s Hot in Paris

**The Latest Dance Craze**  
Paris is always ready to move, and the newest dance obsession is spilling out of studios and into clubs, bars, and pop-up classes across the city. Whether it’s a Latin-inspired routine, electro-chic steps, or a TikTok-born choreography with a Parisian twist, the point is confidence: dress lightly, follow the beat, and don’t worry too much about perfection.

**Le Scrapbooking**  
Yes, scrapbooking has gone très chic. Parisian creatives are turning ticket stubs, café receipts, postcards, pressed flowers, and museum flyers into stylish memory books. Look for stationery shops and weekend ateliers where you can pick up patterned paper, washi tape, stamps, and elegant little embellishments to make your own visual diary of the city.

**Biking Around Town**  
With expanding bike lanes and easy rental options, cycling is one of the best ways to see Paris right now. Glide along the Seine, cruise through the Marais, or pedal from Canal Saint-Martin to the quieter corners of the east. The vibe is practical but romantic: a basket, a scarf, and a stop for a pastry are strongly encouraged.

**Café Hotspots**  
Paris cafés are still the city’s living rooms, but the hottest ones mix old-world charm with modern energy. Think tiny espresso bars, all-day brunch spots, design-forward terraces, and neighborhood cafés where laptops appear by day and wine glasses by evening. The best seat is still outside, angled toward the street, perfect for people-watching.

**Massages at the Mosque**  
For a soothing escape, the hammam at the Grand Mosque of Paris remains a beloved retreat. After steam, scrubs, and mint tea, a massage here feels like stepping out of the city without leaving it. It’s atmospheric, traditional, and deeply relaxing—ideal after a long day of walking cobblestones or exploring museums.

**Subway Style**  
The Métro is more than transportation; it’s a runway with fluorescent lighting. Current Paris subway style is understated but sharp: trench coats, leather jackets, wide-leg trousers, excellent sneakers, crossbody bags, and the occasional flash of red lipstick. The trick is looking effortless while clearly having thought about every detail.
